proposals.relationship: Richter praises Bailyn’s colonial synthesis but challenges language and interpretation that minimize Native settlement, strategic choice and power in shaping colonial migration.
proposals.evidence_note: Own Harvard Magazine review online14December2012/printJanuary–February2013. The objection concerns The Barbarous Years and its peopling framework, not every Bailyn work. Richter explicitly credits James Merrell’s language critique and uses Francis Jennings and Cynthia Van Zandt for the Susquehannock example; retain their credit without inventing endpoints. Praise and disagreement coexist. Bailyn’s full book and any reply remain unread; the apparent PDF link redirects to an accessibility notice, so no print-page collation is claimed.
primary_locators: Harvard Magazine HTML, paragraph beginning Still, for all the book’s learned strengths through the final Native-decisions paragraph; especially word-choice/Merrell, Susquehannock/Jennings/Van Zandt, Pequot War and Thanksgiving examples.

proposals.relationship: Wood uses Richter’s study of Iroquois captive warfare to question Taylor’s account of Native punishment and cross-cultural differences.
proposals.evidence_note: Wood’s own2006 review expressly names Richter’s earlier study in the section2 discussion of captives. This records Wood’s specific scholarly use, not Richter’s endorsement of Wood’s criticism of Taylor. Richter’s1983 War and Culture is a bibliographic lead; Wood does not identify the title, and the match is unconfirmed. The article body and Taylor’s complete book remain unread; the detailed description is Wood’s account. Section1’s separate Facing East discussion and the later unnamed-anthropologists claim are not conflated.
primary_locators: Gordon S. Wood, Apologies to the Iroquois, NYRB6April2006, section2, passage beginning It is surprising that through Taylor reveals none of these details and its punishment quotation.
